shortDescription: From Syria to Carthage, Christians wrote and read stories of Jesus and his apostles under the apostles' own names. Churches read these books aloud, and bishops judged them by what the apostles had handed down.

timeline.headline: Serapion of Antioch lets a gospel under Peter's name be read, then reads it and judges it
timeline.witness: Serapion, in what he wrote to the church at Rhossus, kept by Eusebius

lines.when: in the tenth year of Commodus
lines.text: Eusebius names Serapion, the eighth bishop from the apostles, as bishop of the church at Antioch in these years.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History V.22, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 31003, 31060-31061
lines.note: Eusebius's account, written about a century later.

lines.text: On a visit to Rhossus, a parish in his charge, Serapion supposes all there hold the true faith. Without reading the gospel they put forward under Peter's name, he says that if this is the only thing causing bad feeling among them, let it be read.
lines.reference: Serapion, in Eusebius, Church History VI.12.2-4, cic/texts/eusebius_werke-bd2-2-historia-ecclesiastica-vi-x-rufinus-x-xi-grc-lat_schwartz-mommsen1908.txt lines 2504-2505, 2513-2516; cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 33696-33712

lines.text: Told afterward that the backers' minds were caught up in some heresy, a teaching he held false, he promises to come to them again soon.
lines.reference: Serapion, in Eusebius, Church History VI.12.4, cic/texts/eusebius_werke-bd2-2-historia-ecclesiastica-vi-x-rufinus-x-xi-grc-lat_schwartz-mommsen1908.txt lines 2516-2519; cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 33712-33715
lines.note: The record does not say that he came.

lines.text: He writes that he saw what heresy one Marcianus held, a man who contradicted himself, not understanding what he said.
lines.reference: Serapion, in Eusebius, Church History VI.12.5, cic/texts/eusebius_werke-bd2-2-historia-ecclesiastica-vi-x-rufinus-x-xi-grc-lat_schwartz-mommsen1908.txt lines 2519, 2621; cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 33717-33719, 33738-33739

lines.text: He borrows the gospel from those who had used it from the first, and reads it through. Most of it, he finds, agrees with the Savior's true teaching, but some things have been added, and he sets them out for the church.
lines.reference: Serapion, in Eusebius, Church History VI.12.6, cic/texts/eusebius_werke-bd2-2-historia-ecclesiastica-vi-x-rufinus-x-xi-grc-lat_schwartz-mommsen1908.txt lines 2621-2627; cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 33741-33743, 33812-33815
lines.note: Eusebius does not copy the list of additions.

lines.text: His rule: we receive Peter and the other apostles as we receive Christ, but refuse the writings falsely put under their names, knowing such things were not handed down to us.
lines.reference: Serapion, in Eusebius, Church History VI.12.3, cic/texts/eusebius_werke-bd2-2-historia-ecclesiastica-vi-x-rufinus-x-xi-grc-lat_schwartz-mommsen1908.txt lines 2510-2513; cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 33704-33707

timeline.headline: Tertullian, at Carthage, answers those who cite Thecla's example
timeline.witness: Tertullian of Carthage, in his own On Baptism

lines.when: in the reigns of Severus and Antoninus Caracalla
lines.text: Jerome writes that Tertullian, of Carthage in the province of Africa, flourished in these reigns.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 53, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40496-40499

lines.text: Some cite Thecla's example, from writings wrongly under Paul's name, as leave for women to teach and baptize. Tertullian answers that a woman who takes it on herself to teach gains no right to baptize.
lines.reference: Tertullian, On Baptism 17, cic/texts/tertullian_opera-pars1-lat_reifferscheid-wissowa-csel20.txt lines 12256-12262; cic/texts/anf03_tertullian.xml lines 57770-57782

lines.text: The presbyter in Asia who put the writing together, Tertullian says, was found out, confessed that he had done it for love of Paul, and left his office.
lines.reference: Tertullian, On Baptism 17, cic/texts/tertullian_opera-pars1-lat_reifferscheid-wissowa-csel20.txt lines 12262-12264; cic/texts/anf03_tertullian.xml lines 57782-57789

lines.text: Paul, Tertullian writes, did not even let a woman learn too boldly, so he could not have given her power to teach and baptize.
lines.reference: Tertullian, On Baptism 17, cic/texts/tertullian_opera-pars1-lat_reifferscheid-wissowa-csel20.txt lines 12264-12267; cic/texts/anf03_tertullian.xml lines 57790-57794

timeline.headline: The books tell of Thecla and of Mary's childhood

lines.text: In the Acts of Paul and Thecla, Thecla, a girl of Iconium promised to a man named Thamyris, listens from a window night and day as Paul speaks of virginity and prayer.
lines.reference: Acts of Paul and Thecla, cic/texts/anf08_twelve-patriarchs-clementina-apocrypha-edessa-syriac.xml lines 47762-47767
lines.note: The story as the book's later copies tell it.

lines.text: The governor condemns her to be burned for refusing to marry Thamyris. The book says a cloud full of water and hail puts out the fire, and she is saved.
lines.reference: Acts of Paul and Thecla, cic/texts/anf08_twelve-patriarchs-clementina-apocrypha-edessa-syriac.xml lines 47884-47911
lines.note: A wonder, in the book's own voice.

lines.text: At Antioch, a powerful man, Alexander, seizes her in the street. She tears his cloak and makes him a laughing-stock, and the governor condemns her to the wild beasts.
lines.reference: Acts of Paul and Thecla, cic/texts/anf08_twelve-patriarchs-clementina-apocrypha-edessa-syriac.xml lines 47943-47957

lines.text: In the arena she throws herself into a pit of water, saying that in the name of Jesus Christ she is baptized on her last day.
lines.reference: Acts of Paul and Thecla, cic/texts/anf08_twelve-patriarchs-clementina-apocrypha-edessa-syriac.xml lines 48023-48028; Greek, cic/texts/acta-martyrum-selecta_gebhardt1902.txt lines 10407-10413

lines.text: Paul tells her to go and teach the word of God.
lines.reference: Acts of Paul and Thecla, cic/texts/anf08_twelve-patriarchs-clementina-apocrypha-edessa-syriac.xml lines 48096-48097; Greek, cic/texts/acta-martyrum-selecta_gebhardt1902.txt lines 10538-10540

lines.text: The forms of the book end differently. In one, Thecla goes to Seleucia, enlightens many and falls asleep. In the other, she lives in a cave there for seventy-two years, then goes to Rome and is buried near Paul's tomb.
lines.reference: Acts of Paul and Thecla, Greek, cic/texts/acta-martyrum-selecta_gebhardt1902.txt lines 10558-10559; English, cic/texts/anf08_twelve-patriarchs-clementina-apocrypha-edessa-syriac.xml lines 48109-48121

lines.text: A book under James's name tells of Joachim and Anna, a couple with no child, and of an angel's promise to Anna of a daughter, Mary.
lines.reference: Book of James 1-5, cic/texts/anf08_twelve-patriarchs-clementina-apocrypha-edessa-syriac.xml lines 36612-36628, 36648, 36694-36697, 36729-36736
lines.note: The English is printed from an eleventh-century manuscript. Many other forms of the book exist (lines 36602-36603).

lines.text: At three, the book says, Mary is taken to the temple, and she lives there as if she were a dove, fed from the hand of an angel.
lines.reference: Book of James 7-8, cic/texts/anf08_twelve-patriarchs-clementina-apocrypha-edessa-syriac.xml lines 36784-36799
lines.note: A wonder, in the book's own voice.

lines.text: When she is twelve, a sign marks Joseph to take her into his keeping. He refuses at first, saying that he has children and is an old man.
lines.reference: Book of James 8-9, cic/texts/anf08_twelve-patriarchs-clementina-apocrypha-edessa-syriac.xml lines 36799-36827
lines.note: The copies give her age differently.

lines.text: The book's writer names himself James, who wrote it in Jerusalem.
lines.reference: Book of James, closing lines, cic/texts/anf08_twelve-patriarchs-clementina-apocrypha-edessa-syriac.xml lines 37167-37171

timeline.headline: Origen reports what some drew from a Book of James

lines.text: Origen writes that some, drawing on the Gospel according to Peter or a Book of James, held that the brothers of Jesus were Joseph's sons by an earlier wife. Those who say so, he writes, wish to keep Mary's virginity honored to the end.
lines.reference: Origen, Commentary on Matthew X.17, cic/texts/anf09_gospel-of-peter-diatessaron-origen-commentaries.xml lines 30600-30610
lines.note: Whether his Book of James is the one that survives, the old sources do not say.

timeline.headline: Eusebius sorts the books in his Church History
timeline.witness: Eusebius of Caesarea, in his own Church History

lines.text: Eusebius writes that the Acts, Gospel, Preaching and Apocalypse of Peter were not handed down among the writings of the whole church, since no church writer drew on them.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History III.3.2, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 14462-14463, 14565-14572

lines.text: He counts the Acts of Paul among the rejected writings, books known to most church writers but not genuine.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History III.25.4 and III.25.6, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 18031-18034, 18255-18257

lines.text: The books heretics cite under the apostles' names, among them the gospels of Peter, Thomas and Matthias and the Acts of Andrew and John, he sets lower still. No church writer thought them worth mention, he says, and their style and thought show them to be fictions of heretics, to be cast aside as absurd and impious.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History III.25.6-7, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 18256-18262, 18321-18334

lines.text: Eusebius keeps Serapion's writing on the so-called Gospel of Peter, and copies passages from it.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VI.12.1-6, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 33690-33702, 33815-33816

timeline.headline: The books are judged again, and Thecla's book is read at her shrine

lines.text: Athanasius of Alexandria, in his thirty-ninth festal letter, says that apocryphal writings are an invention of heretics, who write them when they choose.
lines.reference: Athanasius, Festal Letter 39, cic/texts/npnf204_athanasius-select-works-letters.xml lines 68714, 68824-68826

lines.text: Jerome counts the Acts of Paul and Thecla, and the fable of a lion baptized by Paul, among the apocryphal writings. He says Tertullian's presbyter in Asia was convicted by John and resigned his office.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 7, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 39502-39515; the year is a conversion, worked out from Jerome's preface, which takes the work down to the fourteenth year of the emperor Theodosius, line 38785

lines.text: Egeria, a pilgrim from far-distant lands, comes to Seleucia in Isauria. Thecla's church stands on a low hill outside the city, with countless cells of men and women around it.
lines.reference: Egeria, Pilgrimage, cic/texts/egeria_pilgrimage-of-etheria_mcclure-feltoe1919.txt lines 3419-3421, 3757-3759, 3779-3787
lines.note: Her date is the editors' reckoning from her own account.

lines.text: There Egeria finds her friend Marthana, a deaconess, who rules over the cells of the renouncers and virgins.
lines.reference: Egeria, Pilgrimage, cic/texts/egeria_pilgrimage-of-etheria_mcclure-feltoe1919.txt lines 3787-3792

lines.text: Prayer is made at the memorial, and the whole of the Acts of Thecla is read.
lines.reference: Egeria, Pilgrimage, cic/texts/egeria_pilgrimage-of-etheria_mcclure-feltoe1919.txt lines 3815-3819; cic/texts/egeria_pilgrimage-of-silvia_bernard1896.txt lines 9579-9581

lines.text: Jerome writes to a mother that her daughter should avoid all apocryphal writings. If she reads them, she must know they are not by those whose names they bear, and that it takes great discretion to look for gold in the midst of dirt.
lines.reference: Jerome, Letter 107, to Laeta, cic/texts/npnf206_jerome-principal-works.xml lines 20705-20710

timeline.headline: A gospel fragment told in Peter's voice is found in Egypt

lines.text: A fragment of a gospel told in Peter's voice is found in a grave at Akhmim, in Upper Egypt. It is published in 1892.
lines.reference: The editor's introduction to the Gospel of Peter, Ante-Nicene Fathers 9, cic/texts/anf09_gospel-of-peter-diatessaron-origen-commentaries.xml lines 434-440, 784
lines.note: That it is the gospel Serapion read at Rhossus is a modern identification.

uncertain: What the teaching at Rhossus was. Serapion was told only that the backers' minds were caught up in some heresy. He writes that he saw what one Marcianus held, a man who contradicted himself, not understanding what he said. He calls those who had used the book from the first, the successors of those who began it, Docetae. He says no more of what either held, and no other writer of his time ties that name to Rhossus.

What Serapion did next. He promised the church at Rhossus to come again soon, and the record does not say that he came. He set out for them the things added to the gospel, but Eusebius quotes only the lines about his rule and his reading, so the list is lost.

Origen and a Book of James. Origen, in his Commentary on Matthew, reports that some, drawing on the Gospel according to Peter or a Book of James, held that the brothers of Jesus were Joseph's sons by an earlier wife. Those who say so, he writes, wish to keep Mary's virginity honored to the end. Whether his Book of James is the book that survives under James's name, the old sources do not say, and modern editors differ.

Joseph in the book under James's name. When Mary is given to him by a sign, Joseph at first refuses, saying that he has children and is an old man. The text printed in English comes from an eleventh-century manuscript, and many other forms of the book exist.

Eusebius's reasons. Of the books that heretics cited under the apostles' names, among them the gospels of Peter, Thomas and Matthias and the Acts of Andrew and John, Eusebius says that no church writer in the succession had thought them worth mention. Their style, he says, was unlike the apostles', and their thoughts and purpose were so far from true teaching that they showed themselves to be the fictions of heretics.

The presbyter and his judge. Tertullian names no judge, and says that the presbyter left his office. Jerome, nearly two centuries later, says he was convicted by John and resigned his office of presbyter. Jerome also counts the fable of a lion baptized by Paul among the apocryphal writings. In Tertullian's Latin, the words "apud Ioannem", before John, stand only as an early editor's conjecture.

Thecla's end. The forms of her book differ. In one, she goes to Seleucia, enlightens many with the word of God and falls asleep there. In the other, she lives in a cave at Seleucia for seventy-two years, and later goes to Rome and is buried near Paul's tomb.
Thecla's shrine. Egeria writes of numberless cells of men and women around the church, and of a deaconess named Marthana who ruled the cells of the renouncers and virgins.
Egeria. Her name, and the date of her journey in the late fourth century, are editors' reckoning from her own account.

The Gospel of Peter found. A fragment of a gospel told in Peter's voice was found in a grave at Akhmim, in Upper Egypt, in 1886, and published in 1892. That it is the book Serapion read at Rhossus is a modern identification.
The Apocalypse of Peter. The Muratorian fragment, whose date and place are modern reckonings, says that some would not have it read in the church.

quotationOriginals.printed: If this is the only thing which occasions dispute among you, let it be read.

quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Greek is spelled as the scan of Schwartz's print reads: "do- >z00»" stands for δοκοῦν, μιχροφυχίαν for μικροψυχίαν and ἀναγινωσχέσϑω for ἀναγινωσκέσθω. Rufinus's Latin in the same file, lines 2582-2583, confirms the reading: "si hoc est solum, quod inter vos simultatem videtur inferre, legatur codex".
